passage: Transcript, morning briefing, Ferrier and Blum printing works, the wedding job and the press decision. Works Manager Blum: Two items. First, the Considine wedding invitations, which the front office has flagged red. The stock arrived yesterday: the client supplied their own paper, a handmade cotton from a mill they visited on holiday, 300 sheets, no spares, none, and the mill takes eight weeks for more. Pressman Duarte: Handmade cotton on the Heidelberg is a lottery; the sheet thickness varies and she will crumple one in twenty at the grippers, which on 300 sheets with 220 invitations needed is inside our margin but without a single mistake elsewhere. Blum: Alternative? Duarte: The proofing press. Hand fed, one sheet at a time, my hands on every sheet. Slow: two days instead of three hours. But the old press forgives thickness like a grandmother, and I have never lost a sheet on her. Blum: The client is paying for the three hour price. Duarte: The client is paying for 220 perfect invitations from 300 irreplaceable sheets. The two days is what that costs; the question is only who eats the difference. Blum: The shop eats it, this once, and here is the reasoning for the minutes: the mill's name is on the colophon, the couple will tell the mill, and a works that can hand print holiday paper is a works with a story the internet cannot undercut. Also, and mainly, Duarte wants two days alone with that press and has earned them. Duarte: The minutes may say so. Blum: Second item, thirty seconds: the folding machine's part cleared customs, Vogel fits it Thursday, and until then all folding is by hand, for which the bindery requests, and receives, the radio channel of their choosing. Briefing done. Duarte, your paper is in the humidor; the shop watched over it all night, which is a sentence I never expected to say about paper.
question: How many invitations are needed from the 300 sheets?

passage: Minutes, taken word for word at the body's request, Grimswold Allotments and Leisure Gardens, the great manure dispute, special session. Chair Petulengro: Order. The facts, before the feelings, and both will be minuted, this being Grimswold. In March, the association accepted from Hartree Stables a free delivery of forty tons of manure, spread by volunteers across nineteen plots. In June, tomatoes on those plots began fern-leafing, and Mrs. Voskuijl, whose day job is a plant laboratory, ran the test at cost: aminopyralid contamination, the persistent herbicide, entering via the stable's hay supplier, who sprayed a pasture and said nothing. Mrs. Voskuijl: The compound survives the horse, survives the heap, and survives, apparently, everyone's assumptions. Affected: the nineteen plots in varying degrees. The remedy is time, cultivation, and no brassicas or legumes on the worst six plots for two seasons. Chair Petulengro: The feelings, then. Mr. Aldiss, you have the floor and a list. Aldiss: Withdrawn, most of it, after what I heard this morning. I came to demand the stables pay damages. Then I learned that Hartree's own vegetable garden is dead as ours, that the hay man supplied eleven stables, and that young Hartree spent Saturday driving to every one of them with the lab result because, his words, people needed to know before they spread more. You cannot sue a man who is driving. Laughter, and agreement, noted. Chair Petulengro: Motions, then, three, in a row: One, the association joins the county's group complaint against the hay supplier, our evidence pooled, cost nil. Two, a soil test line, 400 dollars annually, enters the budget permanently, because trust is good and bioassays are better; Mrs. Voskuijl will grow the indicator beans. Three, the free manure policy is amended to trust, but ask for the spray records, which will be the motion's official name. All three carried, twenty-two to nil, one abstention from Mr. Grieve, who abstains annually on principle and was thanked for his consistency. Closed at 9:10, tea taken, the fern-leafed tomatoes composted separately, in the flagged bin, as instructed.
question: What contamination did the test identify in the manure?

passage: Transcript, cellar meeting, the Lamb and Compass public house, staff and the new landlady, first week. Landlady Okafor: Short and straight, because the doors open in forty minutes. What changes: three things. What does not: everything else, and I will take questions on both. Change one: the kitchen closes at nine instead of eight-thirty. The last half hour was the kitchen's idea, not mine, so credit where due: Marco says the walkers off the ridge path arrive at twenty to nine, wet and hopeful, and have been eating crisps for supper since the old menu times. Marco: Watching a soaked hiker eat crisps while the fryer cools is a form of cruelty I no longer wish to practice. Okafor: Change two: the snug. It stops being the storeroom it became during the last landlord's, let us say, era, and returns to being a room. The brewery's own 1908 photograph shows it with a fire, settles, and a dartboard, and by the spring it will match the photograph, minus the spittoons, on which point I am firm despite Mr. Tanner's petition. Tanner, potman: The petition was satirical. Okafor: The minutes may decide that for themselves. Change three: the guest ale rotates monthly, chosen by a staff vote, not by whichever rep buys the best lunch, and the first vote happens tonight after close, tasting responsibly, thimbles not pints. What does not change: the prices this year, the quiz on Thursdays, Mrs. Pardoe's tab arrangement, which I have honored as a term of sale and a term of decency, and the dog water bowls, all four, which I am told outrank me in the affections of this village and which I have already refilled. Questions? Marco: The nine o'clock close: does that include Sundays? Okafor: Sundays the kitchen closes at eight, walkers included; the cook also climbed a hill once and wishes to again. Doors in thirty-five minutes. To work, and thank you for staying, all five of you; a pub is its staff, the rest is furniture.
question: At what time do the walkers off the ridge path arrive?

passage: Verbatim record, trustees of the Maddox Bell Tower Preservation Fund, the bat and the bell. Chair Enfield: The situation, for the one trustee who has been abroad: the tower's restoration, fully funded at last after nine years of fetes, cannot begin, because the July survey found a maternity roost of soprano pipistrelles in the bell chamber, 61 bats at the count, and the law is not ambiguous: no works during the roost season, and works outside the season only under license with an ecologist's method statement. Trustee Byrne: How long is the delay? Ecologist, Dr. Amara Cole, by invitation: If the license application goes in this month with my method statement, works can start in October when the roost disperses, and must pause by mid-May. Your builder's schedule fits that window, I have checked with him, provided the scaffolding design changes: the bats' flight line to the east louvre stays open, which moves one scaffold tower and costs, his figure, 800 dollars. Byrne: And the alternative, waiting a full year, costs the winter deterioration and the scaffold price rise, which the builder puts at 4,000. So the bats are saving us money. Cole: I would not put it that way in the license application, but yes. Trustee Mrs. Fabbri: There is a village feeling question. Half the parish thinks the bats have defeated the bells, and the newsletter has been unkind. Cole: Then may I offer what worked at Elmwick: a bat evening. Detectors, the ultrasound made audible, families on the churchyard grass at dusk watching the emergence. At Elmwick the same complainers now run the counts, and the church sells a postcard of the bat over the bell. Sixty-one bats emerging against a sunset is, professionally speaking, better theater than bells. Enfield: Motion: license application this month, scaffold amendment at 800, works October start, and a bat evening in August, Dr. Cole presiding, refreshments by the Fund, postcard rights, the minutes note drily, reserved. Moved Byrne, seconded Fabbri. Carried, five to nil. The bells will ring for Easter over a licensed, counted, and, if the postcard sells, profitable roost. Closed 8:25.
question: How many bats were found at the July count?

passage: Transcript, season planning meeting, Vasterby Open Air Theater, the weather clause. Producer Holm: One agenda item tonight: rain, and what we promise the audience about it. The survey of last season's ticket holders came back: 1,400 responses, and the single biggest complaint, 46 percent of all complaints, is not rain itself but our policy's vagueness, the phrase performances continue in light rain, which, respondents note, has meant everything from drizzle to what one wrote as the night the Tempest became method acting. Laughter. Stage Manager Reyes: The actors' position, which Equity requires me to state: current rules are fine backstage; the stage surface drains well, and we have never had an injury. The costumes are the casualty: the velvets from the winter show cannot take water weekly, and wardrobe spends Mondays drying kings. Holm: The proposal from the front of house team, which I am endorsing: we publish a plain threshold. Performances continue unless rainfall exceeds what the stage rain gauge, mounted where the audience can see it, reads in the interval: 4 millimeters in the hour, and the show pauses; a pause past forty minutes converts every ticket to any other night, no questions, machine-readable at the gate. The gauge makes the rule visible, and visible rules end arguments. Reyes: And wardrobe? Holm: The velvet question is solved by the other line in the budget: understudy costumes in the synthetic, rain designated, switched at the interval if the gauge trends wrong; wardrobe has costed it at 2,800 for the season, against last year's water damage of 3,900, so the rain wardrobe pays for itself in year one. Treasurer Lindqvist: Confirmed, and the refund exposure models at under 2,000 a season on the last decade's weather. Holm: Motion: the 4 millimeter gauge rule, published on every ticket, the rain wardrobe at 2,800, and the gauge itself, the front of house team requests, named. Suggestions were invited, and the winner, from the box office by nineteen votes, is Prospero. Carried, eight to nil. The Tempest, the minutes observe, has claimed its perquisites. Closed 9:00.
question: At what rainfall reading does the show pause?

passage: Minutes in full, the Corve Valley Show, livestock section committee, the judging tent incident review. Chair Strang: The matter everyone has been enjoying since August, formally: the champion ram. The facts. Steward Bickerstaff: Class 14, rams, judged at 11 a.m. by Mr. Elphinstone, champion sash to Woodgate Farm's ram, Ajax. At 2 p.m., a spectator, subsequently identified as the seller of the ram two years prior, remarked in the beer tent that Ajax was not Ajax at all but his brother Achilles, Ajax having, his phrase, retired to the freezer after the fencing incident. The remark traveled at beer tent speed. By 3, the sash was the only calm thing in the sheep lines. Strang: The investigation. Bickerstaff: Ear tag, flock book, and the scrapie testing paperwork all say the shown animal is Ajax. The seller, sober by Tuesday, conceded he could not tell the brothers apart at the trot in any year, and Mrs. Woodgate produced the vet's invoice for the fencing incident: stitches, not freezer. Ajax lives, and won, and is, the vet confirms in writing, extremely alive. Laughter, noted. Strang: So the champion stands. The committee's actual business: the rules gap the affair exposed. Our objection procedure requires protests within thirty minutes of judging, in writing, with a 20 dollar fee. The beer tent, it turns out, is not a recognized channel. Do we change anything? Mrs. Cato: Nothing about the thirty minutes; it protects the judging from exactly this. But I move one addition, from the poultry section's book: the identity of any champion animal is verifiable on request by the steward for one hour after judging, tag against paper, done quietly at the pen. It costs nothing and it would have ended this in August in four minutes. Bickerstaff: Seconded, with the amendment that the verification is announced in the schedule, so its existence is the deterrent. Strang: Carried, seven to nil. The minutes will close by recording the committee's position in full: the ram is the ram, the sash stays, the seller has apologized with a bottle, accepted, and the phrase beer tent speed enters the official vocabulary of this show. Closed 8:55.
question: What did Mrs. Woodgate's vet invoice show the fencing incident required?

passage: Transcript, works committee, Hollowmere Windmill Trust, the sail decision, milling season looming. Chair Prosser: The east sail pair. Report from our millwright. Millwright Dagny Holt: The survey is grim reading: the stocks are sound, but the sail frames on the east pair show rot at eleven joints, wet rot, from the failed paint seasons before this committee's time. My repair estimate: 9,000 dollars, and honesty compels the caveat that opening rotten frames finds more rot roughly always; budget 12,000 and hope to be praised for underspending. New frames to the original 1854 pattern: 16,500, but then those sails are good for forty years with paint discipline. Prosser: The trust holds 13,200 in the fabric fund. Treasurer Ames: And paint discipline, since the phrase has entered the room: the survey attributes this entire decay to perhaps 600 dollars of skipped painting fifteen years ago. I want that arithmetic minuted for our successors: 600 unspent became 16,500 owed. The minutes should frighten them properly. Prosser: Minuted, with the treasurer's relish preserved. The middle course? Holt: There is one, and it is what I would do at my own mill: new frames for the east pair at 16,500, paid over two seasons, the maker holds terms at no interest for heritage trusts, 8,250 each year, which the fund carries. Meanwhile the west pair, which is ten years younger, gets the full paint cycle this summer, 700, so we are never again buying sails because we skipped paint. Ames: The fund carries it with 4,250 to spare in year one. Confirmed. Prosser: And milling? Holt: The mill runs through it all on the west pair alone in moderate winds, two sails, as mills have limped honorably for centuries. Flour for the mill shop continues; the school visits continue; only the photogenic full spread waits a year, and the postcard stock, the shop reports, is in no danger of running out. Prosser: Motion: new east frames on the two season terms, west pair full paint cycle at 700, and a standing paint line in every future budget, titled, at the treasurer's insistence, the 600 dollar lesson. Moved Ames, seconded Holt. Carried, six to nil. Closed 8:40, and the chair notes the mill turned gently throughout, as if listening.
question: How many joints on the east sail frames show rot?

passage: Verbatim minutes, Pendle Row Baths Preservation Society, the mosaic floor discovery, emergency session with the council's conservation officer. Chair Ashcombe: Wednesday's find, for the record: the contractors lifting the 1970s tile in the entrance hall found, eight centimeters down, the original 1896 mosaic floor, largely intact, a wave and dolphin border around a central roundel of, the officer will correct me, a river god. Conservation Officer Pell: A river personification, bearded, holding an urn, and I have seen four of these in a career and never one this complete. The 1970s screed, by pure luck, was laid on a separating layer of sand, so the mosaic released almost undamaged: my assessment is 92 percent complete, with losses confined to the doorway strip where the old turnstile was bolted. Ashcombe: The complication, members, is money and time, as ever, in that order. The entrance hall was budgeted at 8,000 for new tile. Conserving and displaying the mosaic instead: Mr. Pell? Pell: Cleaning, consolidation, and the missing border sections recreated in matching tesserae: 26,000, and the entrance opens three months late. Alternatively, record and re-cover, which costs 2,000, protects the floor for another fifty years, and future generations think what they will of you. Treasurer Grieg: The restoration appeal closed in March at 4,000 over target, and the county heritage fund's officer, whom I telephoned this morning, says a discovery of this class is precisely their emergency category: up to 15,000, decision in six weeks, our case, her words, extremely strong. So the honest gap is 26,000 less our 4,000 surplus less a probable 15,000: 7,000, and three months. Ashcombe: The society was founded to save this building's memory. The building has, with respect to our founding, just called our bluff. Voice from the floor, Mr. Tench, aged, the minutes note, ninety-one: I swam here as a boy and I can tell you why the doorway strip is worn: we queued on it, barefoot, every Saturday of 1938. That is not damage, that is attendance. Put a glass panel over my footprints and charge tuppence to look. Applause. Ashcombe: Motion: conserve and display at 26,000, heritage application tonight, gap funded by appeal reopening with Mr. Tench's sentence as its headline, entrance delayed three months, tile order cancelled. Moved Grieg, seconded the entire front row, the minutes record irregularly. Carried, nineteen to nil. Closed 9:15.
question: What is the officer's assessment of how complete the mosaic is?

passage: Transcript, joint operations meeting, Skerrow Ice Cream and the Skerrow Dairy Cooperative, the milk round revival. Cooperative Chair Bergstrom: The proposal on the table, from our unlikely allies at the ice cream works: a shared electric float, morning milk round for the cooperative, afternoon ice cream round for the works, one vehicle, costs split. Mr. Skerrow, your pitch, briefly. Skerrow: Briefly: my grandfather sold ice cream from a bicycle and your grandfathers sold milk from a cart, and between us we now own forty vans' worth of nostalgia and no vans. The float costs 41,000 electric, plus 3,000 for the cold conversion. Alone, neither business can justify it: my season is April to September afternoons, your milk round is year-round dawns. Together the float works eleven hours a day and the numbers, which your treasurer has checked, land at break even month fourteen. Treasurer Vale: Checked and confirmed, with one correction in our favor: the council's zero emission delivery grant covers 8,000 of the vehicle, bringing break even to month ten. Bergstrom: The doubts, then, so the minutes hold them. Mrs. Ostrander: Refrigeration conflict: milk at four degrees, ice cream at minus eighteen, one cold box? Skerrow: Two compartments, the conversion quote covers both, the engineer's drawing is appended. Mrs. Ostrander: And the branding? A float that says Skerrow Ice Cream delivering the cooperative's milk at dawn confuses the cows and the customers. Skerrow: The signwriter's proposal is appended too: one side each. The float is ours in the afternoon and yours at dawn, and the village gets to watch it change allegiance at noon, which the primary school, who saw the drawing, already call the transformation. Laughter. Bergstrom: Subscriptions from the pre-launch canvass: 118 households signed for morning milk, 60 the minimum the model needed, so the round is viable before it rolls. Motion: joint purchase, 50-50 after grant, operating agreement per the appended draft, service to begin the first Monday of March, and the float, by joint insistence of both boards' grandchildren, to be named the Penguin. Moved Vale, seconded Ostrander. Carried by both boards, unanimous. Closed 8:20, over samples, the minutes admit, of the product.
question: How many households signed for morning milk in the pre-launch canvass?

passage: Minutes, verbatim by standing order, the Quillfast Scriveners Guild, admission of the final apprentice, ceremonial session, open to the public gallery. Warden Amies: Before the ordinary business, the matter the gallery has come for. The guild has trained apprentices in formal penmanship since 1704, and has had, at times, forty at the benches. Tonight we examine one, and she is the only apprentice of any scriveners guild anywhere in the country, which the newspapers have noticed, hence the gallery, whom we welcome and ask not to jog the tables. Clerk of Works Danby: The candidate: Miss Efua Mansah, apprenticed seven years ago at fourteen, presented tonight for her masterpiece examination. The masterpiece, as the ancient form requires: an engrossed document of the candidate's choosing, executed without correction, judged by three masters in silence. Her choosing, the minutes should record, was the guild's own 1704 founding charter, re-engrossed complete, 4,100 words, with the original's two scribal errors, and this is the part the masters wish minuted, reproduced faithfully and then corrected in a scholar's marginal hand, with citations, in the medieval manner of honest emendation. Master Judge Okri: The judgment, delivered as the form insists in one sentence: the work is without fault, the errors are without concealment, and the guild has nothing left to teach her, which is the definition of a master. Warden Amies: The vote of the assembled guild: unanimous, twenty-six voices. Miss Mansah, stand. You entered this hall an apprentice; the door you leave by tonight is the masters' door, third on the left, which has not opened for a new master in nineteen years and was, accordingly, oiled this afternoon. Laughter, and sustained applause, and the gallery, the minutes record with resignation, jogged the tables. Master Mansah, first words as master: I ask that the guild take two apprentices in the new year, and I ask to teach them, and I ask that the advertisement say what the trade truly is: slow, certain, and impossible to automate with dignity. So moved, seconded from every bench at once, carried by acclamation. The ordinary business is deferred to next month, the urn is on, and the 1704 charter, both versions, will hang in the window for the town to compare. Closed, with ceremony, 9:30.
question: How many words is the re-engrossed founding charter?
